message.content:
You are auditing Android/Kotlin AI-agent "skill" files for the "Networking (Retrofit / Ktor)" topic across up to three source repos that are being merged into ONE Claude Code plugin. When multiple skills auto-trigger on the same code, contradictory guidance is a real defect.

Read the FULL content of every SKILL.md in these directories, plus any references/*.md files inside them (use Glob or Bash 'ls -R' first to discover reference files):

- [ahmed] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/everything-claude-code-mobile/skills/ktor-patterns/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [ahmed] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/everything-claude-code-mobile/skills/kmp-networking/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [rcosteira] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/android-skills/plugins/android-skills/skills/android-retrofit/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [rcosteira] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/android-skills/plugins/android-skills/skills/kmp-ktor/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)

Produce:
1. contradictions — cases where two sources give ACTUALLY OPPOSING advice on the SAME specific technical point (not merely different depth or wording of the same principle). Name both sources (labels: "ahmed" / "chris" / "rcosteira"), state each claim, and cite evidence (file path + the specific lines/quote).
2. bugs — code that is broken, will not compile, or is technically WRONG (e.g. catches and swallows CancellationException, loses state across config change, references undefined symbols, wrong plugin/order). severity: critical | major | minor. Cite the file + evidence.
3. depthComparison — which source is most detailed/actionable here and why.
4. uniqueValue — what each source covers that the OTHERS DO NOT (worth keeping regardless of who dominates).

Be precise; cite real file content. Do NOT invent contradictions where sources only differ in depth — that is the most common false positive. Set cluster="networking".

- core:fail-fast: Apply fail-fast error handling — raise immediately on missing or invalid required values instead of returning null/defaults, never swallow exceptions in empty catch blocks, and use typed/custom error classes with actionable context. Use this skill when writing or reviewing error handling, validation, config/parameter reading, try/catch or try/except blocks, or when a defect surfaces far from its cause (works then breaks weirdly later). Trigger keywords — silent fallback, default value, swallowed exception, empty catch, error handling, defensive coding, guard clause. Do NOT use this skill for designing immutable data models (use immutability) or for forward-compatible unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:forward-compat-slots: Apply the forward-compatible reserved-injection-slot convention — a constructor or function parameter prefixed with underscore AND typed optional is an intentionally-unused dependency slot kept so future callers can inject it without touching every call site. Use this skill when adding a dependency to a base class or shared signature that not all implementations use yet, when a composing facade must pass the same dependency uniformly to sub-services, when reviewing an unused parameter, or when deciding whether to delete vs keep an unused argument. Trigger keywords — unused parameter, reserved slot, forward compatibility, optional dependency, _logger, _param, injection slot. Do NOT use this skill for general immutability (use immutability) or fail-fast error handling (use fail-fast).
- core:immutability: Minimize mutability — default domain types to immutable, derive new state with copy-on-write instead of mutating in place, never mutate function arguments, and keep a pure functional core with side effects pushed to a thin imperative shell. Use this skill when designing data models, value objects, or state-transition logic; when reviewing code that mutates shared state, reassigns variables, or mutates passed-in arguments; or when separating business logic from I/O. Trigger keywords — mutable state, in-place mutation, copy-on-write, immutable, frozen, readonly, value object, functional core, shared state bug. - core:pr-authoring: Apply evidence-based pull-request authoring practice — keep each change small (~100-300 lines of substantive change) and single-concern, link the issue so your tracker auto-updates, and follow your team's chosen PR workflow and merge style well. This skill presents the trade-offs of mono-PR vs stacked PRs and squash vs merge-commit rather than mandating one (record your team's pick in .claude/rules/team-conventions.md). Use this skill when opening a PR, sizing or splitting a change, naming a branch, writing a PR description, or deciding mono vs stacked. Do NOT use this skill for reviewing someone else's PR (use pr-review) or for commit-message wording alone.
- core:pr-review: Apply evidence-based code-review practice when reviewing a pull request or diff — calibrate review depth to the change's risk and blast radius, raise one finding per concern, classify each on a Required/Nit/Question severity ladder, and shape each comment as problem-grounded-in-the-diff then why-it-matters then a concrete fix. Use this skill when reviewing a PR, reading a diff, writing review comments, deciding review depth, triaging which findings block merge, or dispatching per-concern review passes. Trigger keywords — review this PR, code review, review the diff, review comment, severity, required vs nit, blocking finding, reviewer. Do NOT use this skill for authoring/sizing your own PR (use pr-authoring) or for running a specific language's linter/typechecker.
- core:secure-coding: Apply OWASP-based secure-coding rules when writing or reviewing code that handles authorization, secrets, logging, external input, persistence, network calls, or mobile local storage — server-side deny-by-default authz on every object/property/function, no hardcoded secrets (centralized store + rotation), never logging secrets/tokens/PII, validate-and-encode all external input, and mobile OS key stores with no plaintext local storage and TLS. Use when adding an endpoint/handler, an auth or ownership check, a logging statement, a DB or shell query, a config/secret read, an IAM policy, or any mobile data-at-rest code. Do NOT use for architecture/layering design or pure language-style/type rules — those have their own skills. Trigger keywords — SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, IDOR, path traversal, insecure deserialization, hardcoded secret, secret in logs, PII leak, sanitize, encode, deny-by-default authz, input validation, TLS, certificate pinning, Keychain, Keystore, clipboard/screenshot leak, key store.
- core:spec-implement: Orchestrate a tiered generator-verifier loop to implement a tightly-specified change cheaply — a strong-tier orchestrator writes the spec and rules, dispatches the cheap-tier executor agent to generate the code, then dispatches the matching strong-tier review agent to verify it, looping until the verifier is clean. Use when you have a SMALL, well-specified, mechanical implementation task (scaffold a component to a schema, boilerplate to a contract, stubs to a spec) and want to route generation to a cheap model while keeping verification strong. Trigger keywords — implement to spec, scaffold, generate to contract, model routing, cheap generate strong verify, generator-verifier, tiered agents. Do NOT use for ambiguous/design work (do it yourself on the strong model), for trivial one-liners (a single strong pass is cheaper than orchestrating), or for pure review with no generation (use pr-review).
- core:testing-behavior: Guidance for writing and reviewing automated tests that catch real bugs — test observable behavior through public APIs, verify resulting state instead of mock call sequences, write tests that survive refactoring, judge suite strength by mutation rather than coverage %, and treat flaky tests as defects. Use when writing unit/integration tests, deciding what to assert, reviewing a test file or PR's tests, debugging a flaky or brittle test, choosing mocks vs fakes, or interpreting a coverage report. Do NOT use for language-specific test-runner setup (pytest/jest/XCTest config) or for non-test code style.
- kotlin:android-architecture: Native-Android app architecture (Google's recommended layered architecture) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android app/feature module code (androidx.*/android.* imports, Activity/Fragment/Service/ViewModel, an :app or :feature module). Covers the UI/domain/data layers and one-way dependency direction Data <- Domain <- UI; single source of truth (the SSOT owns a data type, exposes it immutably, is its only mutator); unidirectional data flow (state down, events up); keeping app logic out of short-lived OS-owned Activities/Fragments/Services; and confining Context/framework classes behind your own abstractions for testability. Triggers — UI/domain/data layer, ViewModel, repository, single source of truth, SSOT, unidirectional data flow, UDF, Activity, Context. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); this is the layering overview, so for depth use android-ui-layer / android-data-layer / android-modularization / jetpack-compose, and for plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-data-layer: Native-Android data layer (repositories + data sources) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android repository, data source, Room/Retrofit/DataStore class, or DI wiring in an app/feature module. Covers the repository as the data layer's only public API (other layers never touch data sources directly); naming (DataType+Repository; DataType+Source+DataSource e.g. NewsRemoteDataSource); one single source of truth per type (offline-first local DB preferred); suspend for one-shot and Flow for streams; immutable exposed models; main-safety via withContext(ioDispatcher) where Dispatchers.IO IS correct (unlike commonMain); errors as Result/custom exceptions; Hilt constructor injection; fakes over mocks. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (Ktor/SQLDelight/Dispatchers.Default — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-interop); for the overview use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, modules android-modularization, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-modularization: Native-Android Gradle modularization (multi-module app structure) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android module boundaries: Gradle build files (build.gradle(.kts) with implementation/api project dependencies), an :app / :feature / :core / :data module, or navigation between features. Covers low coupling and high cohesion; the common module types (app/feature/data/core); the rule that feature modules never depend on other feature modules (the app module mediates, usually via the navigation graph); keeping each module's public surface minimal with Kotlin internal; preferring Gradle implementation over api to avoid leaking transitive deps; and passing primitive IDs (not whole objects) across boundaries. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain source-set layout (a different axis — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-structure); for in-app layering use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, repositories android-data-layer, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-ui-layer: Native-Android UI-layer state holders (ViewModel + UI state) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android ViewModel or screen-level state in an app/feature module (androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel / viewModelScope / StateFlow imports; keywords ViewModel, UiState, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, repeatOnLifecycle, main-safe). Covers the ViewModel as screen-level state holder (survives configuration changes, main-safe, holds NO View/Context/lifecycle reference); modeling UI state as one immutable data class (or a sealed UiState when states are genuinely exclusive); exposing it via read-only StateFlow; and consuming it lifecycle-aware via collectAsStateWithLifecycle (Compose) or repeatOnLifecycle (Views) so collection stops in the background. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); for the overview use android-architecture, repositories android-data-layer, Compose recomposition/side-effects jetpack-compose, Compose-MP UI kmp-compose-mp-ui, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:jetpack-compose: Native-Android Jetpack Compose UI discipline — load when reading/writing/reviewing @Composable code in a native-Android app/feature module (androidx.compose.* imports). Covers state hoisting (stateless composable, value down / events up); recomposition and stability (@Stable/@Immutable, stable params that let Compose skip, unstable collections, stable lambdas); the side-effect APIs (LaunchedEffect and its key restart, rememberCoroutineScope, DisposableEffect/onDispose, rememberUpdatedState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, produceState); remember vs remember(key) vs rememberSaveable; stable keys for lazy-list items; modifier order and the modifier-parameter convention; slot APIs; previews/testing. Do NOT use for Compose Multiplatform / non-Android targets (Skia canvas, UIKitView, iOS/desktop/web — use kmp-compose-mp-ui) or KMP commonMain shared code (kmp-multiplatform); for the architecture overview use android-architecture, ViewModel/UI-state rules android-ui-layer, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:kmp-compose-mp-ui: Depth guidance for Compose Multiplatform UI across non-Android targets (iOS, desktop, web/Wasm). Covers the central fact that Compose MP renders via a Skiko/Skia canvas, not native UIKit/SwiftUI widgets, and what follows (identical look by default, native-view interop, simulated-native iOS scroll physics since 1.8.0, on-device verification of canvas/interop/accessibility); choosing Compose MP vs native UI per target; stability (iOS Stable since 1.8.0, desktop Stable, Web/Wasm Beta); resources, fonts, density; navigation. Use when building or reviewing shared Compose UI for iOS/desktop/web, deciding Compose MP vs SwiftUI/native, debugging gestures or scroll feel on iOS, handling images/fonts/strings, or wiring shared navigation. Trigger keywords — Compose Multiplatform, Skiko, desktop Compose, Compose for Web, Wasm, UIKitView, compose-resources, navigation. Do NOT use for Android-only Jetpack Compose, non-UI logic (use kmp-structure), or Swift/Kotlin interop (use kmp-interop).
- kotlin:kmp-interop: Depth guidance for Kotlin <-> Swift/Objective-C interop and per-platform networking in KMP. Covers refining the ObjC header Kotlin exports to Swift (@HiddenFromObjC, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift), why not to expose Flow directly to Swift (use SKIE) and that suspend->Swift async is officially experimental, exported-surface quirks (top-level funcs become <FileName>Kt classes, generics only on classes, no default args), and Ktor with ktor-client-core in commonMain plus an engine per platform (Darwin/OkHttp/CIO). Use when designing the API a Swift/iOS app consumes from shared Kotlin, debugging an awkward generated Swift signature, deciding how to bridge Flow or suspend to Swift, or wiring the Ktor client. Trigger keywords — Swift interop, Objective-C, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift, SKIE, Flow to Swift, suspend async, Ktor, Darwin, OkHttp. Do NOT use for shared logic structure (use kmp-structure), Compose UI (use kmp-compose-mp-ui), or everyday Kotlin language style (use kotlin-style).
- kotlin:kmp-multiplatform: Kotlin Multiplatform framework rules for shared code — load when reading, writing, or reviewing files under a commonMain or commonTest source set (auto-scoped to **/commonMain/**/*.kt and **/commonTest/**/*.kt), or on demand for KMP layout questions. Covers where shared code lives and the one-way platform->common dependency, what to share vs keep native, the commonMain-only coroutine constraint (Dispatchers.Default not IO, because IO is JVM/Native-only and breaks JS/Wasm), the expect/actual escalation ladder, and commonTest using kotlin.test only (no JUnit, which breaks Native). Keywords — KMP, multiplatform, commonMain, commonTest, expect, actual, source set, Dispatchers in common code, JS, Wasm. Do NOT use for native-Android-only code (there Dispatchers.IO is correct — use the android skills), everyday Kotlin language style (kotlin-style), source-set depth (kmp-structure), Compose-MP UI (kmp-compose-mp-ui), or Swift interop (kmp-interop).

6	# Android Networking with Retrofit
7	
8	Modern Retrofit setup for Android using coroutines, `kotlinx.serialization`, and Hilt. This reference covers the decisions that are easy to get wrong, not the standard boilerplate of service interfaces, Hilt module wiring, and the converter setup.
9	
10	## Service interface
11	
12	Declare every endpoint as a `suspend` function. **Return the body type directly** — Retrofit throws `HttpException` on non-2xx, giving a clean `try/catch` at the repository boundary. Use `Response<T>` **only** when you need the status code, headers, or error body (e.g. server-side validation messages):
13	
14	```kotlin
15	// Direct body — throws HttpException on non-2xx; the common case
16	@GET("users/{user}/repos")
17	suspend fun listRepos(@Path("user") user: String): List<Repo>
18	
19	// Response wrapper — only when you need code/headers/error body
20	@GET("users/{user}")
21	suspend fun getUser(@Path("user") user: String): Response<User>
22	```
23	
24	Wrapping every endpoint in `Response<T>` "just in case" forces callers to check `isSuccessful` and handle a nullable body even when only the body matters — don't.
25	
26	## OkHttp & JSON
27	
28	Standard wiring (in a Hilt `@Module`/`@Provides @Singleton`): `HttpLoggingInterceptor` with its level gated on `BuildConfig.DEBUG`, sensible connect/read timeouts, and the `kotlinx.serialization` converter (`json.asConverterFactory("application/json".toMediaType())`). For an API that's loose with its payloads, configure:
29	
30	```kotlin
31	Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; coerceInputValues = true; isLenient = true }
32	```
33	
34	## Auth: interceptor, and the throw-vs-proceed decision
35	
36	Attach the token via an `Interceptor`, not a per-endpoint `@Header` — a single missed `@Header` parameter is an unauthenticated request that fails at runtime, not compile time. The part most often gotten wrong is **what to do when the token is absent**:
37	
38	```kotlin
39	class AuthInterceptor @Inject constructor(
40	    private val tokenProvider: TokenProvider,
41	) : Interceptor {
42	    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
43	        val token = tokenProvider.getToken()
44	            ?: throw IOException("Auth token unavailable") // fail fast — see note below
45	        val request = chain.request().newBuilder()
46	            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
47	            .build()
48	        return chain.proceed(request)
49	    }
50	}
51	```
52	
53	> **Throw vs proceed:** **Throw** when all endpoints require auth — a missing token should surface immediately rather than silently producing a confusing 401. **Proceed without the header** only if the same `OkHttpClient` is shared between authenticated and public endpoints: `?: return chain.proceed(chain.request())`. Silently proceeding when every call needs auth is a common mistake.
54	
55	## Error handling
56	
57	The repository is the error boundary: catch `HttpException`/`IOException` there and map them to a domain error type — never let Retrofit/OkHttp exception types reach the ViewModel, and never expose Retrofit DTOs to it. Don't redefine the error hierarchy here; see `android-skills:android-data-layer` for the repository pattern and the shared `DataError` taxonomy.
58	
59	## Checklist
60	
61	- [ ] All service functions are `suspend`
62	- [ ] `Response<T>` only when you need the status code, headers, or error body
63	- [ ] `OkHttpClient` logging gated behind `BuildConfig.DEBUG`; sensible timeouts set
64	- [ ] Auth applied via an `Interceptor`, with the token-absent policy chosen (throw vs proceed)
65	- [ ] Network exceptions mapped to domain types at the repository; DTOs never reach the ViewModel
66

5	
6	# Ktor Client for KMP and Android
7	
8	This reference covers the Ktor client configuration traps — plugin install order, serialization flags, auth refresh, and error mapping — not the basics of a shared `HttpClient`, engine selection, or `ContentNegotiation` setup. **Related:** `android-skills:android-data-layer` (repository + the `DataError` error model — its canonical home), `android-skills:android-retrofit` (Android-only equivalent).
9	
10	## Plugin install order — `HttpRequestRetry` BEFORE `HttpTimeout`
11	
12	The install order most often gotten wrong: installing `HttpTimeout` before `HttpRequestRetry`. Plugins run in install order for outgoing requests; retries must be able to catch timeout errors, so retry has to wrap timeout.
13	
14	```kotlin
15	val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; coerceInputValues = true; encodeDefaults = true }  // encodeDefaults: see the section below
16	
17	HttpClient(engine) {
18	    install(ContentNegotiation) { json(json) }
19	    install(Auth) { bearer { /* loadTokens / refreshTokens */ } }
20	    install(HttpRequestRetry) {                 // BEFORE HttpTimeout
21	        retryOnServerErrors(maxRetries = 3)
22	        exponentialDelay()
23	    }
24	    install(HttpTimeout) {                       // AFTER HttpRequestRetry
25	        requestTimeoutMillis = 30_000; connectTimeoutMillis = 15_000; socketTimeoutMillis = 15_000
26	    }
27	}
28	```
29	
30	Reversed, `HttpTimeout` resolves the request as failed before the retry plugin sees it, so timeouts are never retried. (Separately, the `Auth` plugin handles 401 refresh independently — let `HttpRequestRetry` cover transient/5xx failures; don't chain the two around the same status code.)
31	
32	## `encodeDefaults = true` — or protocol-constant fields silently vanish
33	
34	`kotlinx.serialization` defaults to `encodeDefaults = false`, which **strips any property whose value equals its declared default** from the serialized output. A `jsonrpc: String = "2.0"` (or `version = "1.0"`, `type = "..."`) disappears from the payload; the server rejects every request with a generic "invalid request," and the fix is a one-line flag — found only after hours chasing HTTP-layer red herrings. Always set it for client APIs — the `val json` defined at the top of this file does, alongside `ignoreUnknownKeys` and `coerceInputValues`. That one configured instance is what the whole client shares: `install(ContentNegotiation) { json(json) }` and the WebSocket converter both take it.
35	
36	## `expectSuccess` — pick one model, consistently
37	
38	`expectSuccess = true` makes Ktor throw `ClientRequestException` (4xx) / `ServerResponseException` (5xx) on non-2xx — and that throw **runs before any manual status check**, so an `if (response.status == OK)` branch after it is dead code. Pick one model project-wide: `expectSuccess = true` + `try/catch` (matches the repository pattern), or `expectSuccess = false` + explicit `response.status.isSuccess()` inspection. Never mix them.
39	
40	## Bearer refresh — `markAsRefreshTokenRequest()` or it loops
41	
42	In the `Auth` `bearer { refreshTokens { … } }` block, mark the refresh POST with `markAsRefreshTokenRequest()` so it isn't intercepted by the same `Auth` plugin — without it, a failing refresh triggers another refresh, looping infinitely. It's an `HttpRequestBuilder` extension: call it **inside the request builder block**, not bare in `refreshTokens { }` (where it doesn't compile).
43	
44	```kotlin
45	install(Auth) {
46	    bearer {
47	        loadTokens { tokenStorage.getTokens()?.let { BearerTokens(it.access, it.refresh) } }
48	        refreshTokens {
49	            val refresh = oldTokens?.refreshToken ?: return@refreshTokens null
50	            val r = client.post("auth/refresh") {
51	                markAsRefreshTokenRequest()                      // skip the Auth plugin for this call
52	                setBody(RefreshRequestDto(refresh))
53	            }.body<TokenResponseDto>()
54	            tokenStorage.save(r.accessToken, r.refreshToken); BearerTokens(r.accessToken, r.refreshToken)
55	        }
56	        sendWithoutRequest { it.url.pathSegments.none { seg -> seg in listOf("login", "register") } }
57	    }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	Keep `BearerTokens` at the plugin boundary; the rest of the app uses your own token type. `TokenStorage` is project-defined (DataStore on Android/JVM, Keychain on iOS).
62	
63	## WebSockets & SSE — use the serialization converter
64	
65	For real-time transports, install the kotlinx-serialization converter so typed messages flow over the same `Json` config as `ContentNegotiation`; without it you hand-encode/decode `Frame.Text`. (SSE = server→client only, plain HTTP, built-in reconnect; WebSocket = bidirectional, manual reconnect, binary frames — default to SSE when the client only consumes.)
66	
67	```kotlin
68	val client = HttpClient(engine) {
69	    install(WebSockets) {
70	        pingIntervalMillis = 30_000
71	        contentConverter = KotlinxWebsocketSerializationConverter(json)  // the shared configured instance — bare `Json` reverts to encodeDefaults = false
72	    }
73	    install(SSE)
74	}
75	
76	client.webSocket("wss://api.example.com/ws") {
77	    sendSerialized(SubscribeMessage(topic = "items"))
78	    while (true) { val msg = receiveDeserialized<ServerMessage>(); /* handle */ }
79	}
80	
81	// SSE — incoming is a Flow<ServerSentEvent>
82	client.sse("https://api.example.com/events") { incoming.collect { event -> /* event.event / event.data / event.id */ } }
83	```
84	
85	Wrap SSE/WebSocket collection in a `LaunchedEffect` or repository coroutine so cancellation closes the HTTP connection when the consumer goes away.
86	
87	## Error mapping + testing
88	
89	Catch **specific** Ktor types at the repository (`ClientRequestException` / `ServerResponseException` / `HttpRequestTimeoutException` / `IOException`) and map to `DataError` — `catch (e: Exception)` would swallow `CancellationException`. The full repository pattern + `DataError` taxonomy lives in `android-skills:android-data-layer`. For richer per-error UI states (`Unauthorized`, `RateLimited`, `Forbidden`, …), a sealed `ApiResult<T>` + a `safeRequest` wrapper with `expectSuccess = false` is the alternative shape — pick one per project.
90	
91	Inject `HttpClientEngine` so tests swap in `MockEngine`, reusing the production `createHttpClient` factory so plugin config matches:
92	
93	```kotlin
94	val mockEngine = MockEngine { request ->
95	    assertEquals("/users/42", request.url.encodedPath)
96	    respond("""{"id":"42","name":"Ada","created_at":1700000000000}""",
97	        HttpStatusCode.OK, headersOf(HttpHeaders.ContentType, "application/json"))
98	}
99	val repo = UserRepository(UserService(createHttpClient(mockEngine, baseUrl = "https://api.example.com/")))
100	```

input.depthComparison: For the Ktor traps specifically, rcosteira/kmp-ktor is the most actionable: it is organized entirely around the decisions that are easy to get wrong and explains the WHY for each — HttpRequestRetry-before-HttpTimeout ordering (with the rationale that timeout must be wrapped so retries can catch it), encodeDefaults=true (protocol-constant fields vanishing), expectSuccess making post-throw status checks dead code, markAsRefreshTokenRequest preventing an infinite refresh loop, and catching specific exceptions to avoid swallowing CancellationException. It also uniquely covers MockEngine testing and WebSockets/SSE. Its code compiles and is internally consistent. ahmed/kmp-networking is the BROADEST by surface area — it is the only file with full per-platform engine factories, an offline cache layer, a manual retry helper, a full NetworkException hierarchy, an ApiResult sealed wrapper, multipart upload, and Koin DI wiring — but it is shallower on rationale and contains the most defects (CancellationException swallow, a non-compiling OfflineCapableApi, undefined symbols, and a self-violated no-hardcoded-URL rule). ahmed/ktor-patterns is the lightest, Android-only, copy-paste-oriented file. rcosteira/android-retrofit is the only Retrofit reference at all and is tight and correct but scoped to Retrofit. Net: rcosteira/kmp-ktor is the strongest for correctness-per-line and decision guidance; ahmed/kmp-networking wins on raw breadth of scaffolding but needs the bug fixes above before it can be trusted.

uniqueValue.whatIsUnique: OkHttp certificate pinning via CertificatePinner with a documented backup pin (lines 160-175), and an HttpSend request-interceptor pattern for injecting headers like X-Client-Version (lines 146-158). Neither cert pinning nor HttpSend interception appears in any other file.

The only file with concrete per-platform engine factories (OkHttp with a 10MB disk Cache; Darwin session config for cellular/expensive/constrained access and resource timeouts), an offline cache-with-TTL-and-stale-fallback layer, a manual exponential-backoff retryApiCall helper, a full NetworkException taxonomy + Throwable.toNetworkException() mapper, submitFormWithBinaryData multipart avatar upload, an ApiResult sealed wrapper (map/flatMap/getOrElse), Koin DI module wiring, and an explicit DO/DON'T checklist. (Several of these need the bug fixes noted above.)

The only Retrofit coverage in the whole set: suspend service interfaces returning the body type directly (HttpException on non-2xx) vs using Response<T> only when you need status/headers/error body, and the auth-interceptor throw-vs-proceed decision (throw IOException when all endpoints need auth; proceed only for a shared authenticated+public client). No Ktor file covers Retrofit.

Uniquely covers: the HttpRequestRetry-before-HttpTimeout install-order rule with rationale; the encodeDefaults=true protocol-constant explanation; the expectSuccess dead-code-after-throw warning; markAsRefreshTokenRequest to prevent refresh loops; WebSockets vs SSE guidance with a shared kotlinx-serialization converter and cancellation-closes-connection note; and MockEngine testing by injecting HttpClientEngine and reusing the production factory. The pitfall rationale, WebSockets/SSE, and MockEngine testing are absent from the other three.
